note: You are reading the dramatic PLAN for a game, not its finished scenes. The plan is a spine — a theme, a tone, and an optional trope — plus a graph of linear storylines: one main line and, optionally, side lines it branches into. Each storyline is an ordered list of beats (a summary of what happens plus a register and a dramatic job) and ends one of three ways: game_end (a concrete final scene), handoff (hands control back to the line that branched into it), or merge (flows into another line). Judge only the dramatic structure the plan lays out — whether the spine gives the storylines a clear, consistent frame, whether each storyline's beats build coherently and each does distinct work, whether any endings that exist are meaningfully distinct from each other, and whether the register stays consistent with the tone the spine declares. You are not judging prose quality, dialogue, or line-level craft; those are written later. Score on the story's own register — a quiet, low-stakes premise can reach the top level on its own terms, and a plan is never better for reaching for grand stakes. A single storyline with a single ending is a completely valid shape and should be judged on its own merits, not penalized for lacking branches. The top level is a plan a writer would actually build from, not a flawless one. For each criterion, pick the single level (0-4) whose description best matches the plan, and cite the specific storyline, beat, or ending as evidence.

criteria.name: theme_and_tone
criteria._authoring: Replaces central_question_real now that the spine is theme+tone, not a values-fork. A theme WORD or short phrase ('loyalty tested by scarcity') is now a completely fine answer — the old requirement for a forced dilemma is gone. What matters is (1) the theme is legible in what the storylines actually do, not just asserted, and (2) the tone stays consistent — no jokes dropped into a straight tragedy, no whiplash between registers the spine didn't declare (a trope, if present, should also fit).
criteria.description: Is there a clear theme and a consistent, fitting tone that the storylines actually serve — not just a theme asserted in the abstract, and not a tone that lurches?

levels.0: No discernible theme — the spine is a vague or generic label nothing in the storylines connects to — or the tone lurches (a comic beat dropped into an otherwise straight tragedy, or vice versa).
levels.1: The theme is stated but the storylines mostly don't reflect it, or the tone holds most of the time but breaks in at least one storyline in a way that reads as a mistake, not a choice.
levels.2: The theme shows up in some storylines but not others, or the tone is consistent but generic — it doesn't do much beyond not clashing.
levels.3: The theme is legible across the storylines that matter (at minimum the main line), and the tone is consistent and fits the theme and premise.
levels.4: Clear theme + consistent, fitting tone that every storyline visibly serves — you could describe what this story is about from the spine alone and see it borne out beat by beat.

criteria.name: beats_progress
criteria._authoring: Load-bearing — this is the beats_escalate criterion re-scoped to be PER STORYLINE now that beats group under a linear line rather than one global sheet. Judge each storyline's beat sequence on its own: does it build coherently, with each beat doing distinct work (the delete-a-beat test: could a beat be cut and the chain still hold?). Variable length across storylines is expected and fine — a 3-beat side line is not worse than a 15-beat main line for being shorter; judge each on whether ITS beats do real work, not on line length. A storyline that restages the same beat or reports mood instead of a concrete change fails regardless of how many other storylines exist.
criteria.description: Within each storyline, do the beats build coherently, with each beat doing distinct work no other beat in that line does — regardless of how long or short the line runs?

levels.0: Beats restage each other (the same confrontation replayed) or report mood ('tension rises') instead of a concrete change; delete any beat and the chain still holds. True of the main line or of most storylines that have beats.
levels.1: A couple of beats do real work but several are interchangeable or repeat what an earlier beat already established, in the main line or in most side lines.
levels.2: The main line generally advances, but the escalation is uneven — front-loaded, flat in stretches, or a beat or two restates what's already established; side lines (if any) are thin or repetitive.
levels.3: Every storyline's beats each make a specific change no other beat in that line makes; the main line builds toward its terminus and side lines (if any) do real, distinct work in their shorter span.
levels.4: Every beat in every storyline turns its line somewhere new — no line, long or short, could lose a beat without weakening — and the main line's rise is shaped so its heaviest beats land last.

criteria.name: terminal_distinctness
criteria._authoring: Replaces endings_diverge, with the gate REMOVED and the requirement inverted: a single-ending game is now a fully valid shape and should score at the top if that one ending is well-realized — do not penalize a plan for having only one game_end terminus. This criterion only has teeth when there are >=2 game_end endings: they must be more than the same outcome restated. Clusters of similar endings (four different 'you died' scenes in different places) are fine and should NOT be scored as a collapse — collapse means two or more endings are actually identical in substance (same outcome, same stakes, no distinguishing detail beyond cosmetic dressing).
criteria.description: If there are two or more game_end endings, are they distinct from each other rather than the same outcome restated? (A single ending is valid and should be judged on its own merit, not penalized for lacking company.)

levels.0: Two or more endings collapse to one identical outcome — same result, same stakes, distinguished only by cosmetic dressing (a different room, a different line of dialogue) with nothing else that would make a player experience them as different.
levels.1: Multiple endings exist but most are near-duplicates of each other; only one or two feel like their own outcome.
levels.2: Endings are distinguishable but a couple lean on the same underlying resolution with only minor variation (e.g. several are flavors of the same failure state without a clear reason each exists).
levels.3: Every ending is its own outcome — or there is a single, well-realized ending — with no pair reading as interchangeable.
levels.4: A single strong ending, or (if several) a set where each is an unmistakable, distinct outcome that could not be swapped for another without changing what the story means.

criteria.name: tone_consistency
criteria._authoring: Inverted from the old register_variety: variety is no longer the goal, CONSISTENCY is. The spine declares one tone; every beat's register (bonding | comedy | friction | plot | character) should serve that tone rather than clash against it. A story can still use different beat types (a bonding beat, a friction beat) while staying tonally uniform — comedy stays funny throughout, a bleak story stays bleak throughout. The failure is a beat whose register breaks the declared tone (a broad joke landing in the middle of a story whose spine says 'bleak', or a moment of real cruelty in a story whose spine says 'warm and light'), not a lack of variety.
criteria.description: Does the register serve ONE consistent tone across the storylines — comedy staying funny, serious staying serious — rather than lurching between registers the spine doesn't support?

levels.0: The tone lurches badly and repeatedly — jokes dropped into a straight tragedy, or grim cruelty breaking a light story — with no sense the register serves the spine's declared tone at all.
levels.1: Mostly one tone, but at least one storyline or beat clearly breaks register in a way that reads as a mistake rather than a deliberate beat.
levels.2: The tone mostly holds, with one moment that sits slightly off the declared register without badly undermining it.
levels.3: The register stays consistent with the spine's tone across every storyline that matters, even as beat types vary (bonding, friction, plot beats all read as the same story).
levels.4: The tone is uniform and unmistakable everywhere — comedy is funny start to end, or the bleakness never breaks — and every beat's register, whatever its type, reads as serving that one tone.
